Questions

Junk Removal FAQ — Pensacola, FL

This junk removal FAQ for Pensacola, FL gives straight answers to what Northwest Florida homeowners ask us most — about demolition, hauling and tarping alike. First Coast Haul connects you with local partner crews — your estimate and the work itself are handled by the contractor matched to your job.

What items do junk removal companies take?+

Furniture, appliances, mattresses, hot tubs, exercise equipment, construction and yard debris, concrete, dirt, and whole-house cleanout contents are all standard. The exceptions are hazardous materials — paint, chemicals and fuel have to go to the county hazardous-waste drop-off, so set those aside and mention them when you book.

Where can I dump junk myself in Pensacola, FL?+

Pensacola residents can haul to city and county solid-waste facilities themselves — check the City of Pensacola's solid waste pages for current locations, hours and what they accept, and expect to need a truck or trailer and to do the unloading yourself. If you'd rather skip the trips, a crew loads and hauls it in one visit, priced at a free estimate.

How much does it cost to remove a hot tub?+

It depends on the tub's size, whether it's drained and powered off, and the carry-out path — through a gate is quicker than over one. The crew checks all of that at a free on-site estimate and gives you the price in writing before any cutting starts.

Do I need a permit for demolition in Pensacola, FL?+

Usually, yes for structures — Pensacola and the surrounding towns each set their own demolition permit rules, and smaller jobs like interior tear-outs are treated differently from full structure removal. The crew matched to your job flags what's required at the free estimate, and work doesn't start until permits and utility shutoffs are handled.

How long does house demolition take?+

The teardown itself is often measured in days once permits and utility disconnects are cleared; the paperwork and scheduling ahead of it usually take longer than the demo. Your crew gives you a timeline with the written estimate so you can plan around it.

What is selective demolition?+

Selective demolition is taking out part of a structure or interior while the rest stays — one room, a kitchen, flooring, a wall, or one wing of a building. It's the standard approach before a remodel, and it's priced by the exact scope marked at the estimate.

Can I demolish my own house in Florida?+

In some cases an owner can pull permits for their own property, but full house demolition also involves utility disconnects, permit rules, possible asbestos requirements and legal disposal of a very large amount of debris. Most owners who start down the DIY path end up hiring a crew for the teardown and hauling — get a free estimate first and compare honestly.

What happens to materials after demolition?+

The crew sorts as it loads: concrete, metal and clean wood go to recycling where local facilities take them, salvageable items are set aside when agreed, and the rest goes to licensed disposal. The site is left clear and swept — nothing is buried or burned on your property.

How long does a roof tarp last?+

A heavy-duty tarp secured with battens typically holds through weeks of Florida rain and wind — it's temporary protection while permanent repairs are scheduled, not a repair itself. Loose-laid or sandbagged tarps fail much sooner, which is why ours are fastened down.

Will insurance pay for roof tarping?+

Often, yes — tarping is the temporary mitigation most homeowners policies expect after storm damage, and insurers commonly reimburse reasonable tarping costs as part of a covered claim. It isn’t guaranteed: coverage turns on your policy, your deductible and whether the underlying damage is covered. Keep the crew’s before-and-after photos and invoice, file promptly, and confirm the specifics with your insurer or adjuster.

Does homeowners insurance cover roof tarps?+

Often, yes — temporary tarping to prevent further damage is the kind of mitigation many homeowners policies expect and may reimburse, but coverage depends on your policy and your claim. Keep the crew's photos and invoice, and confirm specifics with your insurer or adjuster.

Can you tarp a roof in the rain?+

Not in lightning or unsafe wind — nobody belongs on a roof then. In lighter rain, if the crew judges it safe, tarping can sometimes proceed; otherwise crews dispatch as soon as conditions safely allow. Meanwhile, catch drips in buckets and move valuables out from under the leak.

What size tarp do I need for roof damage?+

Bigger than the damage: a tarp should extend well past the damaged area on every side so wind-driven rain can't get under the edges, and reach over the ridge when the damage is near the peak. Crews size the tarp on site after photographing the damage — that's part of the job, not something you need to measure from the ground.

Does a roof tarp stop leaks?+

Yes — a properly sized, batten-secured tarp is a water barrier that stops rain getting in through the damaged area. It doesn't repair the roof underneath, and edges or new damage elsewhere can still leak, which is why the crew checks the surrounding area while they're up there.

Who do I call for a roof leak at night?+

Stay off the roof at night — it's the most dangerous version of an already risky job. Inside, catch the water, move what's underneath it, and if water is near electrical fixtures, treat that as an electrical hazard first. Then call or text us: tarping calls are dispatched as soon as conditions safely allow, and describing the leak's location inside helps the crew find the entry point fast.

Deconstruction vs. Demolition — Cost and Differences

Demolition takes a structure down as fast as safely possible and hauls the debris. Deconstruction takes it apart piece by piece so materials — lumber, fixtures, doors, brick — can be reused, sold or donated. Deconstruction takes longer and its labor costs more; salvage value and donation benefits can offset some of that, and far less goes to landfill. Demolition is cheaper and faster when there's little worth saving. The honest answer depends on what's in your building.

  • Deconstruction: slower, higher labor, materials salvaged for reuse or donation

  • Hybrid jobs are common: salvage the good material, demolish the rest

How to Tarp a Roof After a Hurricane

Tarping a roof after a hurricane starts with a hard rule: never during the storm, never on a wet or unstable roof, and never alone. Once it's safe, the method that works is a heavy-duty tarp sized to extend well past the damage on every side — over the ridge if the damage is near the peak — with edges wrapped around and screwed through wooden battens so wind can't get under it. Loose tarps and sandbags are the ones in the neighbor's yard after the next band of rain. If the roof is steep, high or badly damaged, this is crew work, not a ladder job.

The short version

  • Wait for safe conditions — no lightning, no high wind, dry footing
  • Size the tarp past the damage on all sides; cover the ridge for peak damage
  • Secure with battens screwed through wrapped edges — never just lay it loose
  • Photograph the damage first, for your insurance file

When a roof leak shows up, the first moves are inside, not on the roof: catch the water, move or cover what's underneath, and check whether water is near electrical fixtures — if it is, treat that as the priority hazard.   • A cover-up is a same-visit fix once a crew can safely get up there

Wind vs. Hail Roof Damage — How to Tell

Wind and hail damage a roof differently. Wind lifts, creases and tears shingles — look for missing tabs, folded-back edges and exposed fasteners, worst on edges and ridges. Hail bruises shingles and knocks off granules — the shingles stay in place but lose their protective surface, and soft metals like vents, gutters and flashing show dents. The distinction matters for insurance documentation, and both kinds of damage leak the same way once rain finds them, so either one is a reason to document and cover promptly.

Call (850) 555-0147 Get a free estimate

The short version

  • Wind: missing, creased or lifted shingles; damage concentrates at edges and the ridge
  • Hail: granule loss, bruised shingles, dented vents and metal trim
  • Photograph soft-metal dents — they're the clearest hail evidence from the ground
  • Both can hide: a roof can look fine from the street and still be leaking

Emergency Roof Repair vs. Replacement

Three different jobs get confused after a storm. A temporary cover (tarping) stops water now and buys decision time. A permanent repair fixes limited damage — a patch of shingles, flashing, a small section — on a roof with life left. Replacement is for widespread damage or a roof already near the end of its life. The emergency move is always the cover; the repair-vs-replacement call comes after inspection, when you're dry and not deciding in a panic.

Call (850) 555-0147 Get a free estimate

The short version

  • Temporary cover: hours, stops the loss, not a repair
  • Repair: right when damage is local and the rest of the roof is sound
  • Replacement: right when damage is widespread or the roof was already worn out
  • Anyone pushing a full replacement before inspecting is selling, not advising
